chunks: Ali, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said: 'The jurists are the trustees of the Messengers, as long as they do not enter into worldly affairs.'
It was said: 'O Messenger of God, what is their entering into worldly affairs?' He said: 'Following the ruling authority. So when they do that, beware of them regarding your religion.'

key_terms.أمناء: Trustees/custodians — those entrusted with a sacred trust (amana)
key_terms.اتباع السلطان: Following the ruling authority — deferring to political power at the expense of religious integrity
key_terms.الرسل: The Messengers — the prophets sent by God
key_terms.الفقهاء: Fuqaha — jurists/scholars of Islamic law, those who possess deep understanding (fiqh) of religion

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet say about scholars who follow the ruling authority?
ai.summary: This hadith, attributed to the Prophet through Imam al-Sadiq's chain, draws a sharp distinction between scholars who remain independent guardians of religious knowledge and those who compromise themselves by aligning with political power. The 'jurists' (fuqaha) are described as trustees of prophetic wisdom, fulfilling the role of prophets in preserving and transmitting revelation. However, when scholars seek patronage from rulers or defer to political authority, they forfeit this sacred trust and become a danger to the faith of the community. The warning was particularly resonant in early Islamic history, when Abbasid caliphs often pressured scholars to issue rulings favorable to state interests.
